comments.name: Vincent Gracco
comments.body:
SNAP spending is falling, but CBO attributes the savings to a combination of stricter work requirements, lower benefits, fewer recipients, and—importantly—shifting costs from the federal government to the states. CBO estimates that the 2025 law will reduce SNAP outlays by $187 billion over a decade, but that is not $187 billion of “waste” eliminated.

Nor does a payment error establish fraud. And the sharp decline in enrollment cannot yet be attributed primarily to rooting out abuse: reporting from the states indicates that documentation requirements and administrative barriers are causing some eligible people to lose benefits.

The relevant question isn't simply “How much did Washington save?” It is “Who ultimately bears the cost of those savings?”

Calling that a successful war on welfare is premature. At this point, the evidence shows a successful reduction in federal SNAP expenditures—not that America has eliminated $187 billion of waste.

Another example of the WSJ ideological framing masquerading as economic/scientific analysis.

comments.name: JAMES tilray
comments.body:
“The Food Stamp Reform Is Working” — based on what measure?

Yes, SNAP spending is below forecast. But spending less isn't proof that fraud was eliminated.

CBO says SNAP spending is falling because Congress expanded work requirements, changed eligibility and benefit calculations, reduced the number of people receiving benefits, and shifted some of the cost to states. SNAP enrollment has already fallen from roughly 42.2 million people to 36.6 million in one year.

There absolutely is fraud and waste in SNAP, and it should be aggressively investigated. USDA has identified billions of dollars in potential fraud, waste and abuse. Go after every dollar of it.

But don't play a shell game with the numbers. Removing someone because they committed fraud is one thing. Removing an eligible person because they couldn't satisfy a new paperwork requirement is another. Reducing someone's legal benefit is another. And shifting part of the bill from Washington to the states is yet another.

All four reduce federal spending.

So before declaring victory, answer one simple question:

Of the dollars that came in below forecast, exactly how much was saved by eliminating VERIFIED FRAUD?

If you can't provide that number, you haven't demonstrated that “policing abuse” produced the savings. You've demonstrated that the government spent less money.

I have not yet read the article, but the many photographs accompanying it gave me pause.
Taken together, the images present Alberta as a bleak, sparsely populated prairie inhabited largely by rugged farmers and solitary individuals living off the land. That is one aspect of Alberta, but far from the whole picture. Alberta also has a sophisticated, urban and globally oriented society, with major cities, universities, cultural institutions and international businesses.
I was also struck by the weather depicted in virtually every image. The skies appear dark and ominous, conveying a persistent sense of foreboding. Was this deliberate? Is the intention to portray Albertans as isolated people leading a hardscrabble existence on an unforgiving landscape?
If so, I think that creates an unfortunate context for an article about Alberta separatism. The separation movement is supported by a minority and should not, in my view, be visually framed as though it represents an inevitable response by an alienated population.
Alberta remains very much a part of Canada and contributes enormously to the country's economic life. Whatever frustrations exist here, Alberta is also part of a nation that strives toward constructive and positive ideals in government and public life.
The photographs left me wondering whether the visual story being told is considerably darker, and narrower, than Alberta itself.

Post 9/11, establishing more robust facility security in places where things can go boom, these background checks are performed annually and are required both by clients and employers as part of continuing employment. Additionally, random drug tests are required for all personnel entering or working in a plant. 

Background checks include name/address/employment data, financial obligations, credit information, legal actions-criminal and civil, traffic violations, court records, etc. The only thing not covered was interviews with friends, relatives, and acquaintances (which usually occur with jobs involving government security requirements).

At the employee level, actionable flags for monitoring, discipline or termination, include legal violence complaints and DUI, and/or a failed random drug test. Monitored, enforced, and quantified in the name of corporate liability, safety, employee and employer security. 

If a sales representative is subjected to this type of scrutiny -- certainly law enforcement, ICE, and DHS, are subjected to even higher standards of pre-employment and continuous employment background monitoring? This is not a question.

comments.name: hope
comments.body:
I really appreciate the section explaining why free speech is so important (including for immigrants), and including a call for dialogue, not censorship. Even though I disagree with your position, I'm glad you agree that people who disagree with are allowed to have their voices heard. 
One thing I would like to mention is that for some people "anti-semitism" means discrimination/harrassment/harm to Jewish people, which is self-evidently wrong. But there are some disingenuous actors who try and claim "anti-semitism" includes any criticism of the Israeli government, which is no true, and in fact cheapens the real anti-semitism that people actually struggle with. Which is to say, I know this article means the former, but some people might interpret it to mean the latter.

comments.name: Flagpole

comments.name: JP
comments.body:
It is almost comical that they are the ones talking about “Western civilization.” One of the central achievements of the "Western civilization" is the principle that the government should have a very limited role in punishing speech. And yes, specifically the government. No one thought freedom of speech meant that a private person had to tolerate profanity in his own home. The distinction was that a private person could ask you to leave; the government could fine you, imprison you, or, in this case, deport you.

People are free to disagree, and people are free to not listen. Perhaps they should be more openminded, but the prevailing consensus was that government regulation on speech would be a cure that is worse than the disease. Or at least that was what was said when it was people like civil rights activists, union organizers, abolitionists that were getting ostracized for their speech.

Yeah, I am not really sure what explains this obsession from some Republicans with portraying “cancel culture” as something historically new or uniquely left-wing, as though intolerance was ever something unique. Intolerance is unjust, obviously. Why not just say that without distorting the history?

One aspect that's important not to overlook is the sheer level of subjectivity.

Demagogues of all political stripes have learned that if you can squeeze someone's words or conduct into the lens of "hate," it all of a sudden becomes much easier to villify and criminalize them.

But "hate" is almost entirely subjective. It's a vibe.  It encompasses things as diverse as irritation, disgust, displeasure, boredom, aggression, and avoidance.

It technically does NOT include criticism, although many people love to squish that in there too, usually because they love to avoid critical thinking.

Going deeper, these four authors have no standing whatsoever in the actions they're criticizing. They don't dictate investment policy or undergraduate student senate authority.  And it's a good thing that they don't, given their naive understanding of investment goals.

Had they demanded that Tufts invest in Palestinian companies, I would be more sympathetic to their demands. The Palestinian Exchange (PEX) has more than 40 Palestinian stocks listed, including pharmaceuticals, banking, telecom, and construction companies.

Tufts should add stamping out ignorance and restraining from shooting from the hip to its graduate required courses. And Trump, Rubio and company should not deport based on innocuous student speech.

comments.name: Fred
comments.body:
I resigned from the ACLU in protest after 44 years of membership because it had devolved from an organization devoted to free speech to one devoted to free speech only by those whom it liked, as well as, in the case of a leader of its LGBTQ rights division, one openly favoring censorship. Instead I joined FIRE, an organization that Mr. French once led.

But I am not optimistic about the future of free speech in America. Just the other day a Times reader commenting on an article declared that those opposed to a host of "progressive" causes were the enemy and deserved no free speech rights at all. This reader seems not to have been paying attention to the news, because in addition to claiming sanctimoniously to be defending free speech, our far-right government has been doing everything it can to destroy it.

It would help if at least a few political leaders of any stature defended free speech and meant it. To some of us, it is as important as cheap gas.

comments.body: When looking at Bond Index funds consider both the share price which can show a gain or a loss, and the total return which includes dividends. Share price * number of shares is the total value of your holding. The share price of bond funds has dropped as interest rates have risen over the last six years. Take Vanguard BND Total US Bond ETF. Looking at the return for last 10 years. The share price high was $89 in July 2020. The price today is  $71.81. About a 14.5% drop. Yikes! But the total return is up 14.25% over that period. That is because interest rates have gone up and reinvested dividends have purchased more shares. Key there is "reinvested". You have not lost anything so long as you have not sold shares. If interest rates drop again the share price will go up but the dividends will be lower. This is for a hypothetical case of purchased shares 10 years ago, held them, value today. But it gives you the picture. You can look up your exact real return or loss at your brokerage. Do not just look at total cost capital gain/loss as that figure includes shares purchased with dividends. An Intermediate term pure Treasury bond fund like VGIT has had a similar drop in share price and a similar positive total return. There is a tax loss harvesting opportunity here. If you are a long term owner of BND or VBTLX you can sell/exchange the shares for VGIT or VBILX. Use the "loss" to offset capital gains from selling some stock fund shares or regular income from interest and dividends.

In 2020, we slashed the maximum allowable sulfur content in marine fuel oil from 3.5% down to just 0.5%. Sulfate aerosols from marine traffic have historically acted as an unintentional planetary cooling shield. Large commercial vessels traditionally burned heavy fuel oil rich in sulfur, which produced immense volumes of sulfur dioxide (SO₂) gas upon combustion. Once in the atmosphere, this gas transformed into highly reflective sulfate particles.

Modeling simulations show that removing sulfate aerosols has added roughly 0.05°C of additional warming to the planet, effectively bringing forward 2 to 3 years of global warming. Maybe we should reverse track and actually increase sulfur content in fuel oil.

I have insomnia, I also have a degree in neuropsychology. 

This article says nothing about dosage or timing. These are critical factors in the complex neurobiology of sleep. Many scientific studies recommend using a dose of no more than 0.3 to 1 mg of melatonin. That is well below the dose you'll find at the drugstore.  

We secrete melatonin from our pineal but as we age this capacity declines. So, supplementing is appropriate. Our bodies also protect us from overdosing. With melatonin, there is a phenomenon called melatonin receptor de-sensitization. If you are taking ten times the melatonin that your body would naturally secrete, you interfere with the bodies endogenous hormonal systems. Low doses are better. And timing matters. It takes some trial and error.

Magnesium is a fascinating biologically active chemical that some believe our system of farming and food processing do not provide us with. Magnesium HAS to be balanced with calcium, or you may find yourself with a new problem: leg cramps. The magnesium we can take in tablets is bound with acids, some of which, like citric acid, promote wakefulness. 

I wish we, as a nation, did do more to study these natural chemicals. Superficial articles like this do not encourage that approach. Before even reading it, I could have predicted that the NYT would demur, and quibble, and then send you back to the pharmaceutical industry.

Surely not because you or your family are well enough off to pay full freight, no need for scholarships or loans. Surely not because a relative graduated at some point ahead of you, or your relative can endow the college with a new football stadium. Surely not because of your gender or race. Surely not because you're a fantastic athlete who can help the university win games and bring in more revenue, as it is not the prime role of higher education to produce olympic-level  athletes.

comments.name: FMcT

When my baby was 2 weeks old, postpartum depression kicked in hard.  I tried to get help, but my husband didn't get it.  My OB/ GYN prescribed a low dose of and SSRI, and I made the earliest appt with a psychiatrist I could find - 6 weeks out. It got worse quickly, and a week or so later I begged my husband to come home from work and take me to the emergency room.  They doubled my medication, prescribed more, I spoke with a psychiatrist, and they set up more psych visits sooner. I wanted them to admit me, so I could sleep, but they wouldn't.  Twenty years later, I look back and see this more clearly - in addition to the hormonal changes, my husband had refused to hire any help.  We had no family nearby- at all - and he wouldn't allow even a part time nanny, thinking that I should be able to do all of it and we couldn't afford it. I had never seen this in him during the long time we'd known each other. Now, we're divorced, and our 20 year old son is thriving, but I still can't believe I survived it.  No one should ever have to go through this kind of isolation, especially when caring for a another human being.  

Why did my husband act this way?  Internalized stigma of mental illness, handed down to him by his old-school Brooklyn parents.

To the women out there getting married and starting families  - always have a savings account that can get you out of immediate danger.  I did not.

comments.body: To me, one of the saddest legacies of 9-11 is what I refer to as Freedom Tower mindset: valuing security above all else and becoming paranoid about one's safety. The Freedom Tower's ten-story blast-resistant base has proliferated in all sorts of other places. Where I live in West Hollywood, I've seen a plethora of security fences and hedges rise where there were none before. I've seen bunker-like dwellings be constructed with blast-proof safe rooms in their innards. I've seen a massive uptick in residents acquiring guard dogs trained to attack strangers. My once incredibly neighborly and accessible neighborhood has transformed into one that is far less pedestrian-focused and far more security-focused. It's a sad development--both in Manhattan at Ground Zero and all over the nation. It's symptomatic of a fear-based culture (which, tragically, has also seen an amplified fear of "the other." That day is indelible -- the sky so blue, the air so clean, the temperature so perfect, the images of women walking, carrying their high heeled work shoes as they themselves were barefoot, walking north with the blankest of looks on their faces. 

I remember an older Asian man, in a window of a small dry cleaning shop on the Upper West Side, furiously ironing something as hundreds of people slowly and silently passed by. I wondered why he was so intent on ironing on that day. 

I can't believe it's been 25 years. I still wonder about him.

comments.name: Alphonso Bedoya

Folks forget that one of the reasons-for-being of the original World Trade Center was to revive Downtown Manhattan commercial development, which had migrated to Midtown after the Depression and WWII. 

The towers suffered a high vacancy rate for years— and were largely occupied by government agencies— until conditions actually did revive over a decade after they were built.

Personally, I thought— along with others, including Ellsworth Kelly— after the attack that the whole site should be left a park… in my case, at or a little above street level with shallow pools (where the towers had been) with glazed bottoms to act as huge skylights over an 80-foot-high memorial space on the base of the “Bathtub.” 

But other sensiblities actually submitted proper proposals and we have what we have today.

Arad’s memorial, at least far exceeds my imagination…

Cities are what they are… and memorial structures and spaces within them are wildly varied in impact and appropriateness— Victor Emmanuel’s in Rome, Lenin’s in Moscow, Jefferson’s in D.C.

It’s tempting to let that last example just hang there; but Arad’s design and Arlington Cemetery are stark contrasts to other development in the nation’s capital.

This was a horrendous tragedy inflicted by a natural disaster probably precipitated by another failure of human custodianship of the only home we have. 
Such widespread destruction from natural disasters seems to be on the rise. It is something I fear in my home town which has been destroyed by storms and earthquakes three times in the past. Perhaps the survival of the green house is a testament to good building practices. When I discussed construction with local experts and town officials I was told that good building practices and regulations are pretty much universal and I witnessed the strong reinforcement of the construction I had done. Unfortunately, safety takes a lower priority for many people whose priority need is a roof over your head and protection from the elements at minimal cost. Safety and permanence are an extra cost that many just can’t afford on their own. Not because they are frivolous spenders or lazy, most are hard working people who just don’t get paid enough to afford anything more. It seems to me that allowing this situation is just another expression of humanity’s failure to take responsibility for the precious resources that sustain us, whether it be the environment or the legions of people that make our lifestyles possible.

“Recently, she fell off a chair and injured herself, and on another night, she urinated on herself at a friend’s house.”

She needs help. Now. What if she drives drunk and kills somebody? 

Being strict is not necessarily the same thing as being abusive.  I don’t see how this girl gets the help she needs without her parents’ knowledge. You need to tell your daughter that you have a moral duty to speak with the girl’s parents. Speak with them compassionately and express concern for the girl’s health and well being. Of course you will not suggest that she needs to be punished, but do stress the need for professional support and counseling.

Thank you for caring for this girl.

I’d recommend talking to the best friend herself.  And by talk, I mean listen without judgement. Listen in such a way that she knows you are a safe adult in her life who she can always come to for guidance & safety. 
As her best friend’s parent, you’ve been in her life a long time already. Tell her directly you are concerned. Ask her what kind of help she wants.

comments.body: You realize this girl is drinking because of her parents.  She’s not rebelling, which is the normal common sense thing is to believe.  She’s building a wall around her emotions so home life is less awful. I think an idea is for a friend and a parenting that friend is to sit down for a chat with her.  Tell her her life at home with strict parents is very temporary.  Try to explain that there are things she can do to become the free person she wants to be - excelling at school, becoming a part of a creative club, or starting a hobby that would be her own that separates her from the stress at home.  She just needs to see this.

comments.body: No! Do not tell the parents. Get help for the girl. There is a reason she is drinking to excess and it could be her parents. Talk with her and even ask your daughter to. comments.name: Stuart Moskowitz
comments.body:
1. Have a long conversation w your daughter about her best friend’s drinking. Tell her of your thinking about contacting her friend’  parents.  
2. Be prepared for denial through minimization or rationalization about your daughter’s friend’s drinking.  Is your daughter concerned herself.   explain to your daughter that her friend is self-medicating and needs some form of professional intervention. 
4,  assess the danger for your daughter. Does she drive with her while she is drunk?  Who drives?  If you suspect a risk to your daughter then you may have to throw caution over to the necessity of  your daughter’s safety. 
5.  Do you have any solid relationship w your daughter’s friend or her parents? Are they able to take in that kind of information. 
6.  If you decide to move forward , remember item 2. Denial. Start with I am concerned about your daughter’s drinking. Are you aware of it?  They might have some big time blowback or surprise they may admit they are aware of it or they themselves may have a drinking as well. 
7,  You can always seek professional advice-and always including your daughter.

comments.name: Michael you
comments.body:
There's no right answer here, unfortunately. Yes to talking to the child and offering support and a safe haven. She needs to know there's at least one grownup on her side. As part of that conversation, LW should try to learn more about her home life (if the girl will share). Are her parents abusive or merely strict? Would they support treatment or insist on punishment? The answers could help clarify the next steps. 

One important consideration here is that early intervention can be invaluable. Even if the parents aren't informed, it's possible LW could help arrange a qualified counselor or connect her with AA meetings focused on older teens (they exist).

That's if it is alcoholism. My daughter had friends in college who drank a lot, sometimes to blackout. So did I. I remember waking up with vomit on my bed from my roommate in the bunk above me. As far as I know my daughter's friends and mine eventually found their way out of it. But it's especially scary at this high schooler's age, and shouldn't be ignored.

I recently complained to Google about an advertisement for a 32 Terrabyte SSD that was being offered for about $70.

I pointed out that no such device actually exists - that it is a total scam.  

I also used some networking tools to investigate the promoters.

The IP of the webserver was clearly a spoof off a Cloudflare IP block, the domain name registration was deficient, and the nameserver information also deficient.   A simple Traceroute to the webserver was still going at over 65 hops when i stopped it.  This is all easy to spot and can only be the result of deliberate obfuscation.

Google's response to me was they had looked at the product, the company, and their own ToS and requirements advertisers for not doing consumer harm and concluded that the product advertising was not a problem and would continue.  

As I mentioned above, no such product, or even close to it exists.  The products you see are fabrications with onboard systems that make it appear as though the product has huge storage capacity, but in fact offer maybe 2 TB at best and wil destroy your data if you use them.

Google relies on the appearance of things looking legitimate.

Raised in part by feminist grandparents, who came of age in the roaring 20s in NYC, I felt "liberated" all my life, but recognized that the world pushed back harder against me for that. 

I recognized early on that not me, but the world had to change.  In one interview (L.S.E.) I was asked if I planned to marry (I had 4 A-level exams), since giving me a place would deprive a man, a breadwinner. I honestly replied that I never planned to marry but would support myself. My class contained a handful of women. We banded together.

In my first year at uni, in the 70s, I became familiar with the feminist movement and attended meetings to help change the system, but was discouraged by the dismissive attitude toward beautiful women; those who refused the uniform of revolution embraced at the time, which was a man's tailored suit; and the prudish attitude which denigrated those who expressed lust for the opposite sex (my Sapphic inclined sisters were considered ipso facto more liberated) Dressing down, looking dowdy, seemed to signify that we weren't "objects" to the leaders of the movement at the time. 

Critics accused Steinem and Germaine Greer of succeeding not on their merits but on their attractiveness. They steered the movement away from the forces of dowdy, stern prudishness.

comments.name: Jonathan
comments.body: There is a surprising omission in this article, both in the text and the photos. The Delhi Metro has proceeded quickly, in large part, because of a brute-force approach that eschews expensive tunnelling in favour of enormous raised railways running down the centre of urban highways. These are held up by immense piers, or you might call them concrete pylons. Each normal pier is about as wide as a small car, but rises three or more storeys above the road - and there are hundreds and hundreds of them dotting the city, with a huge rail deck (viaduct) above every one. I have not been able to find reliable figures, but my guess is that half or even two-thirds of the network has been built on this approach. While I am an admirer of the system overall, and am in awe of how quickly it has been built, readers should be aware that the urban landscape of Delhi has been dramatically overshadowed - quite literally - by these vast concrete behemoths snaking through it. The visual impact has been enormous. If older and more self-conscious cities tried to adopt this cost-effective approach, my prediction is that there would be outrage.

This article seems to cast aspersions on the authenticity of Kusama's later work. Why? 

As for artists managing and producing works to their specifications, though the author for some reason cites only Jeff Koons, anyone who has taken a basic art history course knows of the Baroque and Renaissance workshop system by which works were produced collaboratively with the input of many specialists under the management of a single master, to whom the work was attributed. Try googling the "lone genius" myth, a concept which emerged during the Enlightenment. 

The author also impugns Kusama's capacity to make decisions about her practice on her own, especially in her later years. What's at the bottom of these suspicions? 

Kusama was a successful artist who not only was always forthright about her mental illness, she plainly cited it as the reason for her compulsion to create, to externalize her inner life in the form of aesthetic objects. Her work resonated with a wide audience, and she managed to make a lot of money. 

But this article, though no evidence is provided, seems to want us to doubt that she didn't so much as create her own works herself, and that others secretly managed decisions about its production without her involvement. Why? This is a familiar way of undermining or diminishing a successful woman by questioning her agency, authorship, and legitimacy.

Yes, it’s an astonishing amount of investment spending but what’s being built are transformative technologies. But AI and other forms of advanced computing are likely not going to dissipate as if they’re the tech industry’s and adjacent industries’ equivalent of a fashion trend. 

My hunch: more likely (probability-wise) is that after several years, capex spending and borrowed funding will level off into manageable phases supportive of maintenance, replacement and somewhat routine growth to institute evolutionary adoption of improved designs of hardware, software, connectivity and services. 

While the above is playing out, NOW is the time to consider what strong guardrails need to be deployed (and how & when) regarding the AI realm, including in what manner and where AI centers are deployed.  And to figure out who the guardians might best be and the extent to which regulatory requirements, norms and ethics are established and enforced. 

As part of these developments, serious attention is also needed to ensure the benefits of AI are reasonably and fairly shared broadly across populations and don’t end up essentially in the hands of a comparatively tiny handful of people. 

All of the above is characterized not as a firm prediction but as possible scenarios to be considered.

Gloria was one of my heroines. Way back in college, in 1972, in a sociology class at the Penn State  Harrisburg PA campus, The  male professor asked the class to form into small groups and then pick a relevant current social topic and present it. 
There were 2 other women in that class besides me. (The ratio at this campus was five men to each woman.) I joined the other two women and took on the topic of Women's liberation.  
Each of us then chose to role play a pivotal figure in the Women's liberation movement as a  part of our presentation.  
We then role-played the points and the rationale that best represented the perspective of key leaders of the Women's liberation movement. I proudly researched and then represented Gloria Steinem 's  views.
When the three of us concluded our role presentation in front of the all male class, there was dead silence at first then a few  classmates then clapped. ( We got an A for the presentation at least.)
After class, one of the men came up to me and said, You don't really feel that way , do you?  
Well, Yes, I DO and still do ...Thank You Gloria for fighting to  improve the lives of women!

George Washington fought in many battles and was never wounded. Is Diamond really going to suggest that if Washington had died in the French and Indian War it wouldn't have mattered much? Really?!? Without Washington the Americans very likely would have lost the American Revolution, in which case North American and world history would have been very different.

I think Diamond has it exactly wrong. History is chaotic! Like a ball bouncing down a rocky slope, every rock it hits has the potential to send the ball off in totally different directions -- directions that depend on exactly how the ball hits the rock. Averages do matter of course. Statistically when it reaches the bottom the ball is more likely to come to rest in the middle of the slope than on the extreme left or right. But any result is possible, and every rock the ball hits matters. Every French musketeer who took aim at Washington could have changed the course of history had his aim been a little better. It's the butterfly effect. Any small change today could eventually have great consequences in the future.

Thank you, Mr. Jones.  

For raising a banner as it were and reminding us:  that yes!  

People DO matter.  People are NOT simply pawns and chess pieces moving around on a board--

--shoved about by economic forces or the weather.  

Naturally (as a Christian) i bridle at this rather curt dismissal of Jesus Christ.  I would insist:  no.  He was NOT simply a remarkably charismatic figure (among many)--

--who had the good fortune to be embraced by a Saint Paul. 

Read the four gospels.  And (among many things) note the exclamation that came so many times. 

"No man ever spoke like this man."  He spoke with authority.  An authority that enabled Him to say:  pay attention, folks.  I'm telling you the way it ought to be.  

Remember the lines from Gray's Elegy?  

            "Some mute inglorious Milton here may rest.
              Some Cromwell guiltless of his country's blood."

Horsefeathers! cried American journalist and gadfly, H. L. Mencken.  

"The test of a Milton is that he function like a Milton."  

Which would be my retort to Mr. Diamond.  Lively and engaging though he is.  

You speak of other "great men" waiting in the wings, should the genuine "great man" fail for some reason to show up.  

Produce the doughty guy that would have won the Battle of Agincourt, had there been no Henry V.

Produce the German that would have sparked World War II.  

Trouble is, Mr. Diamond--

--you don't have them.  They're not there.  

Thanks, Mr. Jones.

comments.name: OD

There are few instances of leaders making things dramatically better, but single individuals, given great power, have often made them worse.

One such would be Henry V, whose reign is described here as a "rip-roaring success". He restarted the 100 Years War after 30 years of truce. 

England lost that second, final round of the Hundred Years War even more comprehensively than it had the first, losing vast lands it had held for centuries. 

True, England's defeat came after Henry's death, but he made it inevitable. His fight was carried on by his very capable brother John. But the job was impossible. England lost the first phase of the war despite winning key battles at Crecy and Poitiers. It lost the second phase despite winning key battles at Agincourt and Verneuil. That tells you: France was unconquerable by England. Smart people had drawn that lesson at the end of phase 1 around 1380.

Henry's disastrous war impoverished England, and its failure sparked the Wars of the Roses. So while England and France had enjoyed comparable power and prestige when Henry was crowned, by 1500 France was well on the way to superpower status while England was a backwater.

Already within a few years of Henry V's death, almost all of his victories had been wiped away by someone who really does provide backing for the Great (Wo)Man theory of history. Someone who came from nowhere, with everything stacked against her, and changed history through sheer guts and determination: Joanne of Arc.

I began reading Mr. Horowitz’s article with an unconscious, faintly amused smile on my lips. I made a bet with myself: “I know what he—and The Times—are going to say.” And I won.
That was not surprising, given what I see as The Times’s consistently left-leaning and rather superficial treatment of Spain. The article does not, in my opinion, adequately inform readers about—or fully grasp—the depth and potential danger of the current Spanish situation, not only for Spain itself but also for Europe and, perhaps, beyond.
I would urge The Times and its correspondents to read books and newspapers representing all sides of Spanish life and thought, and to listen to people from across the political and cultural spectrum. Spain is a very old, complex country, and too often The Times seems to approach it with its conclusions already formed rather than with a genuinely open mind.
This is one of the reasons why, during the past few years, I have come very close to canceling my subscription. The many other excellent sections of the newspaper have so far stopped me from doing so.
I hope that by the time we finally reach 2028, The Times will have returned to something closer to normal—and that what sometimes feels like “The Trump Gazette” will have disappeared for good.

As a Spanish reader of The New York Times, I always read its articles about Spain with interest, and I am consistently struck by how positively the country — and, more specifically, its government — tends to be portrayed.
In this case, I was surprised by the reporter’s approval of the willingness shown by some of our politicians to welcome the growing presence of Chinese companies in Spain. Here, it is widely known that this favourable attitude is largely connected to the role played by our former prime minister, José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero, who has acted as a lobbyist for the Chinese government and Chinese companies. Zapatero — whom Americans may also know because of his controversial ties to Venezuela — is currently facing scrutiny over allegations involving corruption and money laundering. It would be good to see The New York Times report on these aspects of Spain as well. When might we expect an article examining the less flattering side of Pedro Sánchez’s government?
I also found it interesting that the reporter described Spain by saying, “This is a place that feels like it’s moving forward,” when the general perception here is precisely the opposite. The country is moving backwards by virtually every measure that directly affects people’s prosperity, with real wages stagnant or even declining for almost twenty years. And that is without even mentioning democratic standards or the rampant corruption affecting the parties that govern us — all of them, without exception.

I think it’s a shame what has happened to the Bay Area. In my view, its economic paradigm has become grotesque and abnormal. I don’t know whether the gap between the wealth and capital accumulated by the tech industry and the rest of the local economy is sustainable in the long run. Tech companies raise massive capital with the help of hedge funds and venture capitalists, and their employees earn lucrative incomes, while living standards for residents outside the industry decline. My guess is that prices for goods, services, and local real estate will likely be inflated even further, as many non-tech workers and local small businesses are expected to get squeezed out or leave the area entirely due to these worsening economic conditions, while the remaining businesses will charge significantly elevated prices by catering primarily to high-income residents.

This raises the question of whether these hedge funds, venture capitalists, and bankers should be allowed to assign arbitrary monetary values to their investments and then simply cash them out, instantly creating billionaires and brand new upper-middle-class millionaires among themselves at will, which ends up causing localized inflation and affordability issues for the general public. Shouldn’t the Treasury Department and the Federal Reserve consider looking into this potentially questionable, quasi-money-printing practice in some capacity?

At any rate, there should be no taxpayer-funded socialization of private losses.

God!"), reflecting the prayerful state of his soul at the time. Gandhiji lived among the "harijan" ("God's people"), the untouchables, on the shores of the Sabarmati River in Ahmedabad. All his life he sought to unify and bring together people of diverse orientations, and he called this (as he titled his autobiography), "My Experiments with Truth." Because the truth is that we, all 8.1 billion people on earth, belong to the same race, have the same DNA, Indians, Pakistanis, Americans, Chinese, Russians, Canadians, and Hottentots -- "It's a One World, after all," as we sang during the World's Fair Exposition in New York City in 1965. comments.name: Jeffrey
comments.body:
Slacklining as a senior might sound too challenging for most of us, but research shows a basic level of balance is crucial for healthy aging.

A 2024 Ontario study of nearly 100,000 adults aged 66 or older found that survival was substantially reduced after hip fractures, especially among older men. 

Fewer than one-third of the men and about half of the women were alive five years after a hip fracture.

Further to that, a major Cochrane review found that exercise focused primarily on balance and functional movements reduced the total rate of falls by 24%.

Not all falls are due to balance issues – low blood pressure, poor vision, peripheral neuropathy, and of course cognitive decline – can all contribute to falls. 

But for most people, basic balance training as we age can pay some big fall-proofing dividends.
